e.etymology: From Arabic hadiyya, a gift. A similar name with a long first a is the feminine of Hadi, guide to the right path.
A modern American coinage with the fashionable -lyn ending, close to Ashlyn, Jazlyn and Adalyn.
From Sanskrit abhaya, without fear, from a-, not, and bhaya, fear. In Hindu and Buddhist art the abhaya mudra, a raised open hand, is the gesture of protection.
A Scottish and Northern Irish surname, from places named Coulter in Lanarkshire and Aberdeenshire. A coulter is also the cutting blade on a plow.
From Slavic bog, god, and dan, given, an early translation of the Greek name Theodore. Bohdan is the Ukrainian and Czech form.
A respelling of Holden, an English surname from a place name meaning hollow valley. Holden Caulfield, narrator of The Catcher in the Rye, made it familiar as a first name.
A modern variant of Adelina, in line with Adalyn and Adalynn. All go back to Germanic adal, noble, by way of Adela and Adeline.

e.meaning: bright man, in the most common spellings
e.etymology: A Japanese masculine name written many ways; aki is most often a character for bright or for autumn, and o one for man, husband or hero.

e.meaning: great trees (also read as rams or strong ones)
e.etymology: A place in the Book of Exodus: the oasis of twelve springs and seventy palm trees where the Israelites camped after crossing the sea. The Hebrew is read as great trees, or as rams or strong ones.
A name used by South Asian Muslim families, usually explained as Arabic idh'an, obedience or willing acceptance.
A spelling of Azariah that follows the Hebrew Azaryah, the Lord has helped. Many Old Testament figures bear it, among them a king of Judah and the companion of Daniel renamed Abednego.

e.meaning: gift; also read as little wolf
e.etymology: The Urdu and Persian spelling of Arabic Uways, a diminutive of Aws, which is read as gift or as wolf. Uways al-Qarani was a revered early Muslim from Yemen, a contemporary of the Prophet Muhammad.
A recent American spelling in the family of Malaya, Malayah and Maliyah. Malaya is the Tagalog word for free, and Malia is the Hawaiian form of Mary.
The Greek and Latin form of Hebrew Azariah, the Lord has helped, as the name appears in older Catholic Bibles. In the Book of Tobit the angel Raphael travels under the name Azarias.
A modern American spelling in the family of Zyir, Zyaire and Zahir. Zahir is an Arabic name meaning bright or evident.

A French short form of Eleonore and related names, usually written with accents and popular in France since the 1990s. Elea was also an ancient Greek city in southern Italy, home of the philosopher Zeno.
Coined in the 19th century, either from Latin vernus, of spring, or as a feminine of Vernon. It was among the hundred most popular American girls' names in the early 1900s.
The American English word buddy, friend, probably a childish form of brother. It began as a nickname and was registered as a given name through the mid-1900s.
e.note: A very common dog name, and an everyday word for friend used to address strangers.

assoc.t: Buddy, Will Ferrell's character in Elf
Buddy Holly, 1950s rock and roll pioneer

e.etymology: A feminine form of Brian that came into regular use in the 1970s. Brian is an old Irish name, probably from a Celtic root meaning high or noble, borne by the high king Brian Boru.
A spelling of Cody, an Irish surname, the English form of O Cuidighthigh, descendant of a helpful person. This -ie spelling has been used more for girls.
A modern American name that follows the sound of Spanish surnames such as Cortez and Martinez. The Mart- part echoes Martin, from the Roman god Mars.
A form of Arabic Samiya, the feminine of Sami, elevated or exalted. In the US it also sits among modern names such as Samiya, Shamya and Tamya.
In most cases not a chosen name: Baby Boy is the placeholder written on records for a newborn boy who has not yet been named, and some of those records were never updated.
e.note: This entry mostly reflects unnamed newborns in birth records, not a name parents picked.

e.etymology: A spelling of Rakim, a name of Arabic character that resembles Karim, Rahim and Hakim. It spread in the US from the late 1980s with the rapper Rakim of Eric B. & Rakim.
A shortened form of Genevieve, the French name of the 5th-century patron saint of Paris, whose origin is uncertain. It was in use in the US in the early 1900s.
A combination of Clara, from Latin clarus, bright or famous, and the ending -belle, French for beautiful.

assoc.t: Clarabelle Cow, Disney character and friend of Minnie

e.etymology: A modern American name in the sound family of Tavin, Tavon and Gavin. It has no settled source.
From Greek Theodosia, the feminine of Theodosius, from theos, god, and a word for giving. Theodosia Burr, daughter of Aaron Burr, is the subject of the song Dear Theodosia in the musical Hamilton.
namesakes: Theodosia Burr Alston (daughter of Aaron Burr, sung about in Hamilton)

assoc.t: Dear Theodosia, song from the musical Hamilton

e.etymology: A spelling of Emily with a doubled l, especially common in Brazil. Emily is the English form of Latin Aemilia, a Roman family name linked to aemulus, rival.

A spelling of Hamza that follows Urdu pronunciation. Hamza, an Arabic name linked with strength and the lion, was borne by Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet Muhammad's uncle, famed for his bravery.
A modern American spelling of Amir, Arabic for prince or commander, written like Jamere and Lamere.

e.meaning: the month of July, named for Julius Caesar
e.etymology: The month name, from Latin Iulius, the month renamed in honor of Julius Caesar. It is used as a word name like April, May and June, and in Spanish-speaking families as a pet form of Julia or Julio.
